source.citation: Thompson, D'Arcy W. (1917) On Growth and Form. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Ch. XVII, 'On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms', pp. 757-759, Figs. 388-393 (figures drawn by Gerhard Heilmann, 1915).
source.license: public domain (author d. 1948; artist d. 1946; published 1917)

claim_text: The pelves of Archaeopteryx and Apatornis (after Heilmann) and intermediate configurations can be found by interpolation between coordinate-transformed forms - i.e. interpolated grids generate biologically real intermediate forms.

quotes.text: ...this process may be especially useful, and will be most obviously legitimate, when we apply it to the particular case of representing intermediate stages between two forms which are actually known to exist, in other words, of reconstructing the transitional stages through which the course of evolution must have successively travelled if it has brought about the change from some ancestral type to its presumed descendant.

In Fig. 390 the outlines of these two co-ordinate systems are superposed upon one another, and those of three intermediate and equidistant co-ordinate systems are interpolated between them. From each of these latter systems, so determined by direct interpolation, a complete co-ordinate diagram is drawn, and the corresponding outline of a pelvis is found from each of these systems of co-ordinates, as in Figs. 391, 392.

Finally, in Fig. 393 the complete series is represented, beginning with the known pelvis of Archaeopteryx, and leading up by our three intermediate hypothetical types to the known pelvis of Apatornis.

state_variables.x = (xi, eta): Cartesian coordinates of the Archaeopteryx reference grid (Fig. 388): 9 vertical lines labelled 1..9, 8 horizontal lines labelled a..h; the pelvis outline is inscribed in this grid
state_variables.phi(x): position in the Apatornis grid (Fig. 389) of the point with reference coordinates x: a smooth, orientation-preserving map of the plane
state_variables.t: interpolation parameter, 0 = Archaeopteryx, 1 = Apatornis; Thompson's three intermediates are t = 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 ('equidistant')
state_variables.Omega_A: the Archaeopteryx pelvis region (ilium + ischium + pubis, acetabulum as interior hole) inscribed in the reference grid

equations.name: coordinate transformation
equations.formula: phi : R^2 -> R^2, phi(grid_A) = grid_B, det(D phi) > 0
equations.source: Thompson 1917 Ch. XVII pp. 727-729 (method) and Figs. 388-389 (this instance)

equations.name: equidistant grid interpolation
equations.source: p. 759 'three intermediate and equidistant co-ordinate systems are interpolated between them' and Fig. 390

equations.name: inscribed intermediate form
equations.source: p. 759 'the corresponding outline of a pelvis is found from each of these systems of co-ordinates' and Figs. 391-393

equations.name: thin-plate spline realisation of phi (modern formalisation of the grid)
equations.formula: phi(x) = A x + b + sum_i w_i U(|x - p_i|),  U(r) = r^2 log r^2,  sum_i w_i = 0,  sum_i w_i p_i = 0
equations.source: Bookstein 1989 IEEE TPAMI 11:567-585 (explicitly built as the mathematical form of Thompson's grids)

equations.name: affine special case (Thompson's 'simple' transformations) and its interpolation
equations.formula: phi(x) = A x + b;  phi_t(x) = ((1 - t) I + t A) x + t b;  det((1-t) I + t A) is quadratic in t and positive on [0,1] when A has positive eigenvalues
equations.source: Thompson 1917 pp. 727-733 (shear, simple strain, oblique transformations)

equations.name: linear-morph identity for corresponding points
equations.formula: if phi(a_i) = b_i then phi_t(a_i) = (1 - t) a_i + t b_i; differences between consecutive equidistant stages are constant: phi_{(k+1)/4}(a_i) - phi_{k/4}(a_i) = (b_i - a_i)/4
equations.source: consequence of E2; this is what 'equidistant' means operationally

equations.name: best-fit stage and equidistance residual
equations.formula: t*_k = <D_k - A, B - A> / |B - A|^2 for drawn intermediate D_k (Procrustes-aligned);  equidistance residual = |t*_k - k/4|
equations.source: this loop (test statistic, not in Thompson)

boundary_conditions.endpoints: phi_0 = identity (Archaeopteryx, Fig. 388); phi_1 = phi (Apatornis, Fig. 389)
boundary_conditions.grid_domain: 9 x 8 reference grid lines; the outline lies strictly inside the grid in both figures
boundary_conditions.orientation: pelvis in left lateral view, anterior to the left (ilium blade dorsal, pubis directed posteroventrally), identical in all five panels of Fig. 393
boundary_conditions.topology: each form is a single connected region with one interior hole (acetabulum); interpolation must preserve this topology

parameter_regime.controls: stage along the Archaeopteryx -> Apatornis transformation

parameter_regime.values: affine (Thompson's simple strains) | thin-plate spline (smooth grid)
parameter_regime.controls: how much of the grid distortion beyond shear/scale is admitted

parameter_regime.values: acetabulum centre + 4 process tips (sparse) | + arc-length semilandmarks between tips (dense, n_per_segment in 8..48)

empirical_claims.claim: The three interpolated forms are intermediate between Archaeopteryx and Apatornis.
empirical_claims.test: Procrustes distance of each drawn intermediate to A and B; best-fit t* strictly increasing in 0 < t*_1 < t*_2 < t*_3 < 1
|t*_k - k/4| small relative to the drawing noise (and vs. a shuffled-t null)

empirical_claims.claim: The intermediate forms follow from the interpolated grids (a reproducible procedure, not free-hand).
empirical_claims.test: linear morph of landmark/semilandmark correspondences reproduces each drawn intermediate better than either endpoint and better than an affine-only interpolation

empirical_claims.claim: The intermediates are biologically real (match actual intermediate Mesozoic bird pelves).
empirical_claims.reason: no 2-D landmark/outline dataset of phylogenetically intermediate taxa (Jeholornis, Sapeornis, Confuciusornis, Enantiornithes, Hesperornithes, Ichthyornis) is pinned here; the pre-scouted Dryad dataset is a variable mismatch (1-D pelvic-canal width). Thompson himself labels the stages 'hypothetical types'.

digitisation.primary_surface: Fig. 393 (p. 760, leaf n779): five wash-drawn silhouettes, dark on cream paper, vertically stacked (top = Archaeopteryx, bottom = Apatornis)
digitisation.segmentation: grayscale -> Otsu threshold (observed 139 on 0..255) -> binary opening (1 iteration) -> connected components -> five largest components (> 50,000 px each at 1904x3128 page resolution) ordered top-to-bottom; the 'GH 1915' signature (2,762 px) and halftone specks are excluded by size
digitisation.landmarks: L0 acetabulum = centroid of the largest interior hole; L1..L4 = the four most prominent process tips (anterior ilium, posterior ilium, ischium, pubis) found as peaks of the boundary's radial distance from L0; semilandmarks resampled by arc length between consecutive landmarks

specimen_photograph.organism: Archaeopteryx lithographica (Berlin specimen, Museum für Naturkunde, HMN 1880/81)
specimen_photograph.author: H. Raab (User:Vesta)

empirical_reference_table.description: Scalar reference values entering the comparison; all are measured by this loop from the pinned Fig. 393 scan unless a literature source is given

rows.value: 21 Mesozoic bird species, pelvic-canal width vs body mass (analogue; mismatch)
